text: Welcome to the Eurofile, a podcast by CSIS, where we look at Europe through a Washington lens. I'm your host, Max Bergman. Hello and welcome back to the Eurofile. Today's episode is the second part of my interview last month with Henry Foy, the Brussels bureau chief for the Financial Times. In the first part of our conversation,

we discussed what was on the fall agenda in Brussels and which key issues Washington should be watching. If you haven't listened to that episode, go check it out. The link will be in the show notes. Today, we'll dive into the Brussels media landscape from Henry's personal experience at the FT, how national media and coverage of the EU converge, and what makes covering Brussels different from any other city. As a journalist covering EU affairs and leading a team of reporters focused on European politics and policy in Brussels, Henry is the perfect help us

understand this really unique media landscape. And it really also reveals something about Brussels and the European Union as well. We hope you enjoy the show. >> [music] >> Henry, I sort of want to shift gears um and and talk about your experience and time in Brussels. You've been in Brussels for 5 years, so since since COVID. How how has it been as a journalist first of all in Brussels? Is

it hard to get stories? Um are people skeptical of journalists? How would you compare it perhaps to some of the other capitals in London and Moscow and others that you've you've operated in? >> I mean, look, I think Brussels is a great place to be a journalist for for for one key reason, and that's in every single meeting room there are at least 27 people. And for most of those 27, it's not a do or die situation, and so they're quite keen or at least not that bothered in telling

you what happened in that room. It is a It is It is a a city of files, and what I mean by that is that sort of whatever file matters is the one that dominates, but that means there's all sorts of files being being thrown around the other committee rooms, which people are quite happy to share. So, as a journalist, it is a good place to go fishing. The The The European Union has a very open attitude towards media freedom, which is a wonderful thing. I think some of their political leaders wish that they weren't so open, but no, I can't

complain about that. The It's also great to work for an institution at the Financial Times that really cares about the EU, and I mean that in a in a very serious way. The FT has always prioritized its Brussels coverage both in terms of policy, but also now increasingly geopolitics and geoeconomics. And even as a British-headquartered [clears throat] Japanese-owned institution, the Europeans are very kind to us here, and I think

I think Brussels has changed a lot, and we we can talk a bit about that, but it is still a place where the European Commission wants the world to know what's happening here. So, therefore, they are open to journalists. They are open to talking to us, and in general, they are very happy to explain things and and and and to get their message out. And there's enough journalists here to do that. >> It seems like one of the challenges, though, is that well, there's everyone, you know, 27 people in a room,

you can get the source, you can get get the document, but then you have to explain the document. >> Yeah, that's the hardest [laughter] part. >> The hardest part. So, there's access, there's a transparency, but then there's also a density to to Brussels. And how do you approach that? That How do you, you know, the multi-annual financial framework, you know, explaining Eurospeak? You know, is that something that is sort of overrated, or is that like a key challenge that that all Brussels-based journalists sort of

confront in making the EU decipherable? >> I mean, look, at the FT, we our readers are are are typically quite rich, but they're typically quite time-poor. They do not want to read, you know, seven stories a week on the MFF. They want to read that one story in a month that explains why it matters, which direction it's going, and how it might affect their stock portfolio, their geopolitical positioning, their research on a certain topic. So, my job really, and and and my

brilliant team here, is to look at the the issues, look at which ones matter, look look which ones are ripe. You know, you could write stories on every single topic every single day here, but but most of them aren't moving on very much. It's picking the time to write the story so that the reader understands why it's important. One thing I would say on documents is that be very, very wary of media organizations that just publish a document raw online. That is basically the journalist giving up and saying, "I can't work out why you should care about this document. I'm just going to throw

it online, and and you can read it, or or you can get your AI platform to read it." But but I mean, we get here we get so many documents here, right? And I say to my team, "Look, like if you can't tell me what's interesting on you about this document, then you certainly can't write it in a story, and a reader is certainly not going to care." So, it's about picking the timing, making sure the file is ripe and important, and then explaining why it actually matters to somebody who frankly doesn't live and breathe the Schuman roundabout.

>> Maybe we could talk a little bit about how the media landscape has evolved in Brussels, how you see it, where the FT sits in it. You know, Brussels is oftentimes covered by foreign correspondents, and I mean that both, you know, here in the US with reporters in in Brussels, but also within Europe, you know, papers in Madrid and Rome will send their reporters to Brussels to say what's what's important, what matters to Italians, to Spaniards, or to Poles. So, what is the the kind of Brussels bubble

from a media perspective? What How is it evolved? What is it like? Where does How does the FT sort of sit in it in that ecosystem? >> Yeah, that's a great question. I mean, I think I divide it up into four groups. You have the national the national media outlets as you just said, TV, radio, print, um who who sort of coalesce in their groups. You know, there's sort of 50 to 60 odd accredited Germans, 40 to 50 French, Italians, you know, and they're writing about what's happening here from a national lens, you know, for their

editors back home in in Rome or or or Paris and certainly for their readers who care. And so, the Dutch guy at the press conference is always going to ask about how much things are going to cost. Cuz that's what the Dutch care about. Uh the French the French girl is always going to ask about, you know, buy European and like is this anti-Trump or whatever, you know, I'm doing my colleagues a disservice, but you get the drift. Then there's the the the international media who care about Brussels as a place and and write about what happens here in and of in and of

Brussels itself. And and that's that's Politico, that's Euractiv, that's Euronews. These are sort of big newsrooms, you know, sort of 60 to 90 journalists who are writing about Brussels for Brussels. Then there's international guys, the US papers, Chinese it's third country who do write about it sort of in Europe, this is what the Europeans are thinking, you know, so very much sort of like New York Times writing about London, you know, in the

old world. Um so so and and the FT sort of sits in between those two in the middle, right? We're small, we have I have a newsroom here of of six. So so we don't we don't compete scale-wise with with with the Euro with the Euronews's or the or the Politico's or whatever, but we also don't write about Brussels like the Wall Street Journal does, which is sort of A quite infrequently compared to us and B sort of as a foreign country. And then the fourth category is is the guys that make

enormous amounts of money doing specialized coverage, you know, MLex, the sort of competition bubble people, the sort of chemicals that some you know, these news wires you've probably never heard of, but they specialize on one topic and they charge an exorbitant amount of money to their to their clients who who don't who don't care about the MFF. They just want to know if that one regulation on that one new titanium dioxide compound is going to be approved and if it does, that that means millions of dollars in more sales. And

so Brussels matters for all four of those groups in different ways and the ones that succeed are the ones that know exactly who their audience is and therefore exactly what they should be writing about. The ones that fail sort of are trying to look at the other three and think, oh, they're writing about that. That's interesting. We should do that too. And actually like FT readers don't care about titanium dioxide compounds, but they also don't care about like, oh, the the head of the you know, the competition unit in this country's embassy has just been sacked

and they're going to you know, take a job somewhere else in the commission. So there's so much to write about and it it's just like DC, right? You have specialized media for certain things, but then there's this added benefit of the national media who are sometimes covering things in much better ways than than and it's certainly the way that we should because they're looking at it from an Italian angle or from a Hungarian angle or from a Spanish angle and they bring stuff out that others miss because they're because they're thinking about it from a national capital. >> Can I ask you about language? Uh you

know, the FT, an English paper, is that a big advantage? Have you found that English seems to be or is basically the working language of Brussels? Um and >> don't don't say that anywhere near the French embassy. >> I do. I do. I just I deliberately just shout at them in English. But I mean, I've seen a statistic that 90% of the legislation out of the commission originates in English. Is English I mean, so so push back on the premise. I mean,

but is English the sort of working currency of Brussels, and that's how I think Politico kind of comes at Brussels as well, writing in English, and and trying to get a pan-European audience that of Europeans who increasingly read, speak, tweet, in English. Have you found that are you reaching more and more across Europe? Is there sort of a pan-European media interest in Brussels that that you're covering because you're writing in the language that is the frankly Europe's

second language? How do you see that? >> Yeah, I mean, look, officially, and I should state this for the record, the language of the European Commission is French and English, which means the midday briefings, you can ask questions in French or English, the spokespeople had to do both. You know, the president can speak both. Ursula von der Leyen, who was born in Brussels, she speaks perfect French. So so there are both. However, in practice, English is the one that that dominates, and even though the Brits have left, and technically the only country in the EU that uses English as the official language is Malta, one

of its smallest, if not the smallest. I should know that. But the problem is all of these other countries, particularly the the Nordics, the Baltics, and the Eastern countries that joined post-2004, post- Warsaw Pact countries, all taught their diplomats in English. So you have an entire generation of EU diplomats who speak English. And so when there was this slight push, not official, but sort of kind of quite official from the French post-Brexit to be like, maybe we just make it French.

Uh a lot of these countries were like, no way. Uh because, you know, we we can't train an entire generation to also speak French. Does English give us an advantage? Yeah, definitely. Uh mainly because as media in general across Europe, but across the Western world, is eroded, and you have smaller newsrooms in other countries, they are going to have people in those newsrooms who can read English, and so therefore see an FT headline and pick that up in a way that they won't see a Le Monde headline and fully understand it, maybe, or or a Spanish newspaper or

a German one. It definitely helps with with with the reach. Um I'd also say that, you know, just generally with with with social media, with the way that news is now spread, with platforms, um translation to English is is is ubiquitous. And and most young people are going to be versed in English as well. So, yeah, it it helps. I mean, look, I get the comments all the time, right? You know, this English newspaper, what why does it have so much influence in in Brussels? And, you know, you look at the the annual influence tables, it's

always us, it's always Politico, Bloomberg, Reuters, The Economist. I mean, there's a reason why why the English language media uh is doing that. One thing that always amazes me is that why didn't a French businessman set up a French language kind of FT equivalent in Brussels because, you know, 40 years ago uh because it would have been a no-brainer. But, of course, the problem was they were all investing in French newspapers. >> Mhm. >> Or Belgian newspapers. And um and that that hasn't that hasn't taken off on the same in the same way.

However, you know, there is an advantage, of course, speaking to national diplomats and even officials in the commission in their native tongue. They they may well be more um chatty. They may want to share more information with their countrymen. In our bureau, we have, you know, at least a dozen European languages. Um so so we're we're kind of covered, but um it's it's definitely advantage to to be writing in English. And and you you notice now that so many of the quotes and the comments and the prepared remarks from these from these uh

officials are always prepared in English plus another language. >> Maybe a final question. How would you say your 5 years, how how has the Brussels media environment evolved? How is how have you seen Brussels evolve? Maybe not just the media environment, but Brussels evolve. How do you sort of maybe project out the next 5 years? Is the commission growing in stature? Is there more focus on Brussels than there was maybe 5 years ago? is that is the media landscape changing in a in

dramatic ways. Are there sort of new challenges to how you get information? I mean, we don't need to go into all the the challenges that confront the media business, but I'm just curious how you see maybe from a Brussels vantage point how things have have evolved in the 5 years and how you see it headed. >> Yeah, I mean there's there's been a surge of investment into Brussels new outlets, new new competitors, people focusing on this city as a way to write the European story, which makes sense, right? I mean, this is not Washington D.C. in the same way

that the states feed into D.C. A lot of a lot of power is still very much held in the national capitals of Europe, but you can put a correspondent here and they can have a pretty good sense of what's happening in Europe. So, you've seen a lot of people a lot of startup media invest here. That's made it more more dynamic, it's made it more competitive. Second thing, the Russian war against Ukraine has changed the dynamic of this town completely. NATO, which used to be this backwater where you'd have sort of one correspondent covering it and they'd go once a month and you know, they're doing great stuff and they're protecting Europe, blah blah

blah blah, but it was a lot of kind of just going through the motions. NATO exploded in importance and you now have correspondents who go there every day. You have whole, you know, some of my competitors have sort of teams of four or five people accredited to NATO who who will be going for all the events. So, that's brought another side to the city the European Commission becoming more of a defense player and and Europe just kind of trying to find a way to deal with as we said China, the US and Russia all at the same time has made the the city more

exciting, I think, to outside readers because it matters. You know, this is the future of Europe stuff and and the the war in Ukraine story, it's not a brilliant story, it's it's a terrible story, it's a tragic story, but it's a story that we have found readers at the FT who are a cynical bunch, I tell you Max. I mean, they they they like to make money and they can have can have quite questionable views sometimes. The readership numbers on our Ukraine stories have not fallen off one bit in in, you know, in in four and a half years of conflict because it is a good

versus evil story. It is a it is a a simple idea that one big country invaded a small one. There's lots of other stories around support for Ukraine and and support for Russia and all that kind of stuff, but the the core story and I think that drew a lot of people to the to the Brussels bubble media scene. In the future, I think a lot of it depends on politics in member states. I mean, as so the European Union goes, as so the Brussels media scene. If you get far-right leaders in France,

potentially Spain, parts of Germany, let's see what happens in Poland, Italy, and the Eurosceptic movement becomes properly aligned and people start actually pull bits out or just seize up the way this city works, which is possible. Every country has a veto. You start having three or four Victor Orbans, um then Brussels will become a much less interesting place to cover. And I think that could be a point where the media dynamism here, which has sort of been

steadily increasing from sort of 2020 onwards, will will will fade off again. Um let's see. I hope that doesn't happen, um but uh it's it if you can if you can find out what is happening here that makes sense to the rest of the world, it is a really interesting place to be a journalist. And like I said earlier, it is a place that supports journalism, that wants openness, that is willing to talk. And as you look around the world at other major

uh geopolitical players, that's not always the case. >> Henry, this has been a fantastic conversation.
